The Electromotive Force

Chapter 26 treated a battery as an ideal source of constant potential difference. The electromotive force (EMF), \(\mathcal{E}\), is the energy the battery gives each unit of charge that passes through it — the potential difference it maintains when no current flows. Despite its name, EMF is not a force; it is a voltage, measured in volts. The name is older than the distinction between force and energy.

Real Batteries and Terminal Voltage

A real battery has internal resistance \(r\) — the resistance of the chemicals and electrodes the current must pass through. We model it as an ideal EMF \(\mathcal{E}\) in series with \(r\), connected to an external load \(R\):

Step 1 — the energy supplied. Each coulomb that passes through the battery gains energy \(\mathcal{E}\) (Chapter 24: a potential difference is energy per unit charge).

Step 2 — one current. The battery’s interior and the load are in one unbroken path, so by Chapter 26 they carry the same current \(I\).

Step 3 — the drops add. The coulomb gives up \(Ir\) inside the battery and \(IR\) in the load — the two-wires-end-to-end result of Chapter 26. It returns to where it started, so the energy gained equals the energy given up:

\[\mathcal{E} = Ir + IR\]

Step 4 — solve.

\[\boxed{\;I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r}\;}\]

The terminal voltage — what a voltmeter across the battery’s terminals reads — is the drop across the load, \(IR\):

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E} - Ir\;}\]

Check the limits.

  • Open circuit (\(R \to \infty\)). \(I \to 0\), so \(\Delta V_\text{term} \to \mathcal{E}\). With no current there is no drop inside the battery — which is why the EMF is defined at zero current.
  • Short circuit (\(R \to 0\)). \(I \to \mathcal{E}/r\), finite, and \(\Delta V_\text{term} \to 0\). A real battery cannot deliver infinite current, and all its power is dissipated inside it as heat. This is why short circuits are dangerous.
  • Ideal battery (\(r \to 0\)). \(\Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E}\) at every current — the Chapter 26 model, recovered.

The Power Budget

Multiply Step 3 by \(I\):

\[I\mathcal{E} = I^2R + I^2r\]

The left side is the power the EMF delivers; the right side is where it goes — into the load and into the battery itself. This is Chapter 26’s \(P = I^2R\), applied to both resistances that share the current.

The compressed-air canister. The canister’s internal pressure plays the EMF — the most driving pressure available. The nozzle is the load: a narrow nozzle (large \(R\)) lets little air out and holds the outlet near full pressure. Open it wider (smaller \(R\)) and more air flows, but the outlet pressure drops, because more of the canister’s pressure is spent pushing air through its own internal passages (the internal resistance \(r\)). Fully open (\(R \to 0\)), the flow is as large as the canister can sustain and the outlet pressure is zero — the short circuit.

Property Ideal battery Real battery
Internal resistance \(r = 0\) \(r > 0\)
Terminal voltage \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E}\) \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir\)
Power to load \(P = \mathcal{E}I\) \(P = \mathcal{E}I - I^2r\)
Short-circuit current \(\infty\) \(\mathcal{E}/r\)

Example: Terminal Voltage Under Load, and an Aging Battery

A battery has \(\mathcal{E} = 12.0\) V and \(r = 0.050\ \Omega\). It is connected to a load \(R = 3.00\ \Omega\).

Step 1 — the current.

\[I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r} = \frac{12.0}{3.00 + 0.050} = 3.93\ \text{A}\]

Step 2 — the terminal voltage.

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V_\text{term} = 12.0 - (3.93)(0.050) = 11.8\ \text{V}\;}\]

Step 3 — the power budget. To the load, \(I^2R = 46.4\) W; inside the battery, \(I^2r = 0.77\) W. The battery delivers 98% of its power to the load.

Step 4 — the same battery, aged. Its EMF barely changes, but \(r\) rises to \(2.00\ \Omega\). Now \(I = 12.0/5.00 = 2.40\) A, the terminal voltage falls to \(12.0 - (2.40)(2.00) = 7.2\) V, and the internal loss is \(I^2r = 11.5\) W — 40% of the \(28.8\) W the EMF delivers.

Check the budget. Aged: \(I^2R + I^2r = (2.40)^2(3.00) + 11.5 = 17.3 + 11.5 = 28.8\) W \(= I\mathcal{E}\). An old battery “dies” not because its EMF is gone — a voltmeter on the bench still reads nearly 12 V — but because its internal resistance eats the terminal voltage as soon as a current is drawn.

*Personal note: This is why car batteries feel warm after cranking a starter motor. The starter draws hundreds of amps, and \(I^2r\) losses are substantial.
